hook.text: You think you see the world as it is. But your brain is inventing most of what you experience.

buildup.text: Sensory signals are noisy and incomplete. Your retina has a blind spot and your vision is sharp only in the center.

discovery.text: Perception fills in the gaps using expectations, memories, and assumptions. You see a best guess, not raw data.

twist.text: This is why illusions work. They exploit the brain's shortcuts and assumptions to create experiences that aren't there.

climax.text: Helmholtz called perception 'unconscious inference'—the brain making thousands of tiny bets every second.

punchline.text: You don't see reality—you see your brain's best guess.

details.summary: Perception is not a passive recording of reality but an active construction by the brain. Your visual system fills in blind spots, constructs edges, and invents colors. What you see is a best-guess model built from fragmentary sensory data, not a faithful photograph.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding that perception is constructed, not received, changes how you think about eyewitness testimony, disagreements, and the nature of reality itself.
takeaways: The brain actively constructs perception from partial data
What you see is a model, not a direct copy of reality
Perceptual construction explains many illusions and errors

faq.question: If perception is constructed, is anything we see real?
faq.answer: Your perception is a useful approximation of reality, accurate enough for survival. It captures structure and patterns that matter for action. But it is filtered, compressed, and interpreted.

faq.question: Why did the brain evolve to construct perception?
faq.answer: Sensory data is noisy, incomplete, and ambiguous. Raw processing would be too slow for survival. The brain uses prior experience and expectations to fill gaps and resolve ambiguity instantly. This constructive approach trades perfect accuracy for speed and usefulness in real-world action.
